# The Internet Gold Rush {#sec-4-11}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act IV — The Silicon Valley Machine · 1993–1999
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** How does a research network become a commercial empire?

**The answer.** By being handed over. The network was built with public money
for thirty years and then commercialised in about thirty months, and the
question that drove the era was who would own the interface between people and
information. Netscape and Yahoo both came out of universities; both were funded
from Sand Hill Road; and both were answers to a question that search would
answer better.

**The mechanism.** Public subsidy converted into private monopoly, in the most
literal form in the book: a federally funded network transferred to commercial
operation. Then chokepoint control contested — browser, portal, directory, and
finally search.

**The key fact.** Netscape's browser descended from Mosaic, developed at a
federally funded supercomputing centre at a public university. The company that
opened the commercial internet was built on software the public had already paid
for.

**The human anchor.** Marc Andreessen, a student programmer on a federal grant,
becoming the face of an initial public offering that had no profits and was
worth billions by the afternoon.

**Excluded voices.** The public that funded the network's construction and
received no equity in its commercialisation, and the retail investors who bought
the top of the bubble. Also the alternative architectures — public, municipal,
or common-carrier — that were foreclosed without being debated.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that thirty years of public network investment
was converted into private ownership without compensation by tracing Mosaic's
funding to Netscape's valuation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

Mosaic, the browser that made the web usable, was written at a federally funded
supercomputing centre at a public university. Netscape was built on its
foundations, went public in August 1995 without profits, and was worth billions
by the afternoon. Thirty years of public network investment were converted into
private ownership in about thirty months, and the chapter traces the funding
line from the grant to the valuation.

The handover itself received almost no public deliberation. The National Science
Foundation backbone's acceptable use policy had restricted commercial traffic;
it was lifted, the backbone was decommissioned in 1995, and the network passed
to commercial operators. Alternative architectures — common carriage, municipal
provision, public utility treatment — were foreclosed without being seriously
debated, and the chapter names them because their absence was a choice.

What followed was a contest over the interface between people and information,
which is the same position the mission register held in Act II and the operating
system held two chapters ago. Netscape held the browser. Yahoo, built by two
Stanford graduate students on university machines, held the directory. Both were
answers to the right question, and both were about to be beaten by a better one.

Portals lost for a structural reason rather than a competitive one: human
curation does not scale with the web's growth rate, and a directory of the
internet becomes impossible somewhere around the point it becomes useful.

The bubble mechanics belong to the previous chapter's capital chokepoint
operating in public markets that would buy anything — underwriting practices,
lock-up expirations, and retail investors arriving last.

The public that funded the network received no equity in its commercialisation.
That is the chapter's ledger entry, and it is the largest single instance of the
book's second mechanism.

Search is the chokepoint, and two Stanford doctoral students have already
published the paper.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}

   signalled.
4. **Yahoo, 1994-95.** Yang and Filo, a directory built on Stanford machines.
   The portal as an attempt at the chokepoint.

   information — the same position the mission register, the railroad timetable,
   and the operating system each occupied.

   public markets would buy anything. Underwriting, lock-ups, and flipping.

   rather than narrating the horse race.
8. **The excluded.** No public equity in a public asset; retail investors at the

:::

::: {.chapter-question}
How does a research network become a commercial empire?
:::

Mosaic, the browser that made the web usable by people who were not already
computer scientists, was written at the National Center for Supercomputing
Applications at the University of Illinois, on federal funding, and released
free in 1993.

Netscape Communications, founded the following year by one of Mosaic's authors
and by Jim Clark of Silicon Graphics, went public on 9 August 1995. It had
minimal revenue and no profits. The shares had been priced at fourteen dollars,
were doubled to twenty-eight before the offering on the strength of demand, and
closed the first day at more than double that again.

Thirty years of publicly funded network development were converted into private
ownership in about thirty months, and the chapter traces the line from the grant
to the valuation.

## The handover

The network had been built with public money since ARPANET's first four nodes in
1969, and by the early 1990s the National Science Foundation operated the
backbone that connected American research institutions.

That backbone carried an acceptable use policy prohibiting commercial traffic.
Commercial networks existed alongside it, and pressure to interconnect had been
building for years. The policy was progressively relaxed, and in April 1995 the
NSFNET backbone was decommissioned and the network passed to commercial
operators.

The chapter's observation is about the process rather than the outcome. This was
among the most consequential infrastructure decisions in American history, and
it was made almost entirely through agency policy, appropriations language, and
technical committees, with no significant public debate about the alternatives.

There were alternatives. The network could have been operated as a regulated
common carrier, as the telephone system had been. It could have been maintained
as a public utility with mandated interconnection. Municipal provision was
possible and was later attempted in various places and frequently blocked by
state legislation. None of these was seriously argued in public before the
question was settled.

The public built an asset over three decades and transferred it without
compensation, without equity, and without a conversation.

## What the contest was about

The commercial question of 1994 to 1999 was who would own the interface between
people and information, and every significant company of the period was an
answer to it.

Netscape held the browser, which was the obvious position: everyone reaching the
web passed through it, and the company assumed that the browser would become the
platform on which applications ran. Microsoft, which had missed the internet
entirely in its early planning, recognised the threat to the position it held
from chapter 9 and bundled Internet Explorer with Windows, which destroyed
Netscape's revenue model and produced the antitrust case of 1998.

Yahoo held the directory. Jerry Yang and David Filo were Stanford doctoral
students, and their guide to the web began on university machines in 1994 as a
list of links they had found useful. It grew into a hand-curated hierarchical
directory and then a portal — news, mail, finance, chat — on the theory that the
way to hold the audience was to be the place they started.

## Why the portal lost

Directories failed for a structural reason rather than a competitive one, and
the reason is worth stating because it explains the shape of everything after.

Human curation does not scale with a network that is growing exponentially. A
directory of the web becomes impossible at approximately the moment it becomes
essential, because the labour required to maintain it rises with the size of the
thing being catalogued while the value of any individual entry falls.

The alternative was to abandon curation and rank algorithmically, and the
question then became what signal to rank on. Keyword matching was easily gamed
and by 1997 the results of most search engines were substantially spam.

Two Stanford doctoral students working on a digital library project had a better
signal, and the next chapter is about it.

## The mechanics of a bubble

The capital chokepoint from chapter 5 behaved in a specific way once public
markets would buy anything, and the mechanics are worth setting out because they
recur.

Venture firms funded companies at increasing valuations on the expectation of a
public offering rather than of profitability. Investment banks took those
companies public quickly, on small floats that constrained supply and produced
dramatic first-day rises. Insiders were subject to lock-up periods that
prevented them selling for some months, which meant the price was set by a thin
market of new buyers. Analysts at the same banks published favourable coverage.

Retail investors arrived last, buying at the top from the people who had bought
early. When the NASDAQ peaked in March 2000 and then lost roughly three-quarters
of its value over the following two and a half years, the losses fell
disproportionately on those buyers, while the venture firms and the banks had
largely realised their positions.

The chapter should also state the other half honestly, because the bubble is
usually treated as pure waste. Enormous quantities of fibre optic cable were
laid during these years by companies that went bankrupt, and that capacity —
bought at a fraction of its cost by whoever picked up the assets — is the
physical infrastructure on which the following two decades of internet growth
ran. The capital was destroyed and the cable stayed in the ground.

## Amazon, and the model that survived

One company from this period established a pattern worth marking because Act V
depends on it.

Amazon went public in 1997 and lost money for years, deliberately, reinvesting
everything into growth and infrastructure while its founder told shareholders
repeatedly that this was the plan. The market eventually accepted the argument
that scale in a network business is worth more than near-term profit, because
the firm that gets there first acquires a position competitors cannot assault.

That proposition — grow first, monetise later, and accept losses indefinitely to
secure a chokepoint — becomes the standard operating assumption of the platform
era. It is only rational if the position at the end is genuinely defensible, and
the extraordinary thing about the following twenty years is how often it was.

## The Stanford channel

The corridor supplied the founders for this wave as reliably as it had supplied
them for the last, and the mechanism is worth naming because it was becoming
formal.

Yang and Filo were doctoral students. Their directory ran on university
machines, on university bandwidth, until the traffic became a problem and they
were encouraged to move it. Cisco had been founded in 1984 by two Stanford
administrators who had built equipment to connect the campus's incompatible
networks, and it took the university's technology under licence. Sun
Microsystems had been founded in 1982, its name an acronym for the Stanford
University Network, on a workstation design developed on campus. Silicon
Graphics came out of a Stanford laboratory in 1982.

Four of the significant infrastructure companies of the era came directly out of
one university's computer science and engineering departments within fifteen
years, and in each case the university had a licensing or equity relationship.

That is Bayh-Dole from chapter 10 operating as designed, and it is the loop from
chapter 1 running at full speed. Federal research funding produces technology
and people. The technology is patented by the university. The people found
companies to commercialise it. The companies lease space nearby, hire the next
graduates, and fund the next research. And the university takes a position at
every stage.

By the late 1990s the arrangement was so well understood that founding a company
had become a recognised outcome of graduate study rather than an alternative to
it.

## What is now in place

By 1999 the network is private, the browser war is over, the portal has lost,
and the bubble is about to end.

What has been established is that the interface between people and information
is the most valuable position in the economy, and that whoever holds it can be
worth more than the companies whose products pass through it.

The remaining question was what the interface would be, and the answer had been
published in a graduate paper the year before, complete with a warning about
what would happen if its authors did what they were about to do.
